title: Cross-Linguistic Rhythmic and Spectral Feature-Based Analysis of Nyishi and Adi: Two Under-Resourced Languages of Arunachal Pradesh
comment: Submitted to Sadhana (Indian Academy of Sciences); currently under consideration
summary: Under-resourced languages remain underrepresented in quantitative rhythm research,particularly in systematic intra-branch analysis of acoustic differentiation within closely related linguistic groups.This study investigates acoustic differentiation within the Tani language subgroup by examining speech rhythm in Nyishi and Adi,two under-resourced Tani languages spoken in Arunachal Pradesh,North-East India,using a frequency domain framework based on amplitude modulation(AM) low-frequency(LF) spectrum analysis,commonly referred to as rhythm formant analysis(RFA).The analysis is designed to identify whether intra-branch differentiation follows a hierarchical pattern across rhythmic and spectral domains.From the LF modulation spectrum,three rhythm formant features were derived:Number of Dominant peaks(NDP),Mean Frequency of Dominant Peaks(MFDP),and Variance of Dominant Frequencies(VFDP).In addition,Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT)coefficients and Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficient(MFCC) were extracted to characterise the spectral modulation structure and broad spectral organisation of the speech signal.Statistical modelling reveals a hierarchical pattern of differentiation,where rhythmic features show consistent but moderate separation,with Nyishi exhibiting higher dominant modulation frequencies as well as greater dispersion than Adi.Classification experiments further support this hierarchy,with rhythm-only features achieved approximately 84-85% classification accuracy.Fusion using MFCC representations improved performance to 90.9% classification accuracy using support vector machine (SVM) and 93.96% using multilayer perceptron (MLP).These findings demonstrate that rhythmic and spectral features encode complementary levels of linguistic variations,with low frequency modulation capturing constrained macro temporal structure and spectral features reflecting finer phonological differentiation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates acoustic differentiation between Nyishi and Adi (under-resourced Tani languages) using rhythm formant analysis (AM low-frequency spectrum) and spectral features (DCT, MFCC), finding hierarchical differentiation: rhythm features yield ~84-85% classification accuracy, while fusion with MFCC improves to ~94% (MLP), demonstrating complementary roles of rhythmic and spectral domains.
AI.motivation: Under-resourced languages are underrepresented in quantitative rhythm research, and systematic intra-branch acoustic differentiation within closely related linguistic groups has been insufficiently studied.
AI.method: Rhythm formant analysis (RFA) based on amplitude modulation low-frequency spectrum to extract NDP, MFDP, VFDP; plus DCT coefficients and MFCC; classification using SVM and MLP.
AI.result: Rhythm-only features achieved ~84-85% accuracy; fusion with MFCC improved to 90.9% (SVM) and 93.96% (MLP). Nyishi showed higher dominant modulation frequencies and greater dispersion than Adi.
AI.conclusion: Rhythmic and spectral features encode complementary levels of linguistic variation: low-frequency modulation captures constrained macro-temporal structure, while spectral features reflect finer phonological differentiation, forming a hierarchical differentiation pattern.

title: Huí Sù: Co-constructing a Dual Feedback Apparatus
comment: Accepted for publication at the International Conference on New Interfaces for Musical Expression (NIME) 2026 (music track)
summary: This performance presents a duet between two intelligent musical instruments, Sù (to trace back; to go upstream) and Agentier (playing on agentic clavier), and their human performers, connected through feedback loops. Rather than treating AI as a tool that responds predictably to input, both systems operate recursively, where past actions continuously influence future behaviour. The Sù operates in the audio space through latent representation. Its performer uses Make Noise 0-series synthesisers and MIDI controllers to work with a neural feedback synthesis system based on a RAVE model, with a latent feedback loop embedded within the model's internal structure. This allows the instrument to remember and reuse its own internal states, influencing ongoing sound generation through its recent sonic history. The Agentier functions in the control space. Its performer interacts with the system using a Roland S-1 synthesiser and Keith McMillen QuNeo touchpad, where control gestures are routed into a recurrent neural network that feeds back into the synthesis process. Through this feedback loop, the system actively shapes the evolution of control signals over time. Contrasting feedback in the audio and control domains, the performance explores shared agency, resistance, and negotiation between humans and intelligent musical systems. Musical phenomena are co-produced through the entangled states of interaction, rather than through pre-existing system configuration or fixed mappings.

AI.tldr: A live performance featuring two AI-powered musical instruments (Sù and Agentier) with recursive feedback loops in audio and control domains, exploring human-AI co-creation and shared agency through entangled interaction rather than fixed mappings.
AI.motivation: To challenge the paradigm of AI as a predictable tool in music by designing systems where past actions recursively shape future behavior, enabling genuine co-creation and shared agency between humans and intelligent instruments.
AI.method: Two systems: (1) Sù operates in audio space using a RAVE neural model with embedded latent feedback loop, controlled via Make Noise 0-series synths and MIDI controllers; (2) Agentier operates in control space using a recurrent neural network that feeds control signals back into synthesis, controlled via Roland S-1 and Keith McMillen QuNeo touchpad. Both systems exhibit recursive behavior where past states influence ongoing generation.
AI.result: The performance demonstrates co-produced musical phenomena arising from entangled human-system interactions, with contrasting feedback behaviors in audio and control domains that illustrate shared agency, resistance, and negotiation.
AI.conclusion: AI-based musical instruments can function as co-creative agents through recursive feedback architectures, moving beyond fixed mappings and tool-like responsiveness toward dynamic, negotiated human-machine collaboration.

title: ASAP: An Azimuth-Priority Strip-Based Search Approach to Planar Microphone Array DOA Estimation in 3D
comment: This paper has been accepted to the Fourteenth IEEE Sensor Array and Multichannel Signal Processing Workshop, 2026
summary: Direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation is an important task in microphone array processing and many downstream applications. The steered response power with phase transform (SRP-PHAT) method has been widely adopted for DOA estimation in recent years. However, accurate SRP-PHAT estimation in 3D scenarios requires evaluating steering responses over thousands of candidate directions, severely limiting real-time performance on resource-constrained platforms. This challenge becomes even more critical for planar arrays, which are widely used in robotics due to their structural simplicity. Motivated by the fact that azimuth estimation is usually more reliable than elevation estimation for most arrays, we propose ASAP, an azimuth-priority strip-based search approach to planar microphone array DOA estimation in 3D. In the first stage, ASAP performs coarse-to-fine region contraction within azimuthal strips to lock azimuth angles while retaining multiple maxima through spherical caps. In the second stage, it refines elevation along the great-circle arc between two close candidates. Extensive simulations and real-world experiments validate the efficiency and merits of the proposed method over existing approaches.

AI.tldr: ASAP is a fast azimuth-priority strip-based search method for 3D DOA estimation with planar microphone arrays, achieving real-time performance by first estimating azimuth through coarse-to-fine region contraction within strips, then refining elevation along the great-circle arc between top candidates.
AI.motivation: SRP-PHAT-based 3D DOA estimation is computationally expensive due to evaluating thousands of candidate directions, making real-time performance difficult on resource-constrained platforms like robots, especially for planar arrays which are common but have inherent estimation asymmetries.
AI.method: A two-stage azimuth-priority search: Stage 1 performs coarse-to-fine region contraction within azimuthal strips to lock azimuth while retaining multiple maxima via spherical caps; Stage 2 refines elevation along the great-circle arc between the two best candidates.
AI.result: Both simulations and real-world experiments demonstrate that ASAP achieves superior efficiency and accuracy compared to existing approaches for planar microphone array 3D DOA estimation.
AI.conclusion: ASAP enables real-time 3D DOA estimation on resource-constrained platforms by exploiting the fact that azimuth estimation is more reliable than elevation for most arrays, using a strip-based search that dramatically reduces computational cost without sacrificing accuracy.

title: ML-SAN: Multi-Level Speaker-Adaptive Network for Emotion Recognition in Conversations
comment: Main paper (12 pages). Accepted for publication by International Conference on Intelligent Computing 2026
summary: To establish empathy with machines, it is essential to fully understand human emotional changes. However, research in multimodal emotion recognition often overlooks one problem: individual expressive traits vary significantly, which means that different people may express emotions differently. In our daily lives, we can see this. When communicating with different people, some express "happiness" through their facial expressions and words, while others may hide their happiness or express it through their actions. Both are expressions of 'happiness,' but such differences in emotional expression are still too difficult for machines to distinguish. Current emotion recognition remains at a 'static' level, using a single recognition model to identify all emotional styles. This "simplification" often affects the recognition results, especially in multi-turn dialogues. To address this problem, this paper introduces a novel Multi-Level Speaker Adaptive Network (ML-SAN), which, specifically, effectively addresses the challenge of speaker identity information confusion. ML-SAN does not simply assign a speaker's ID after recognition; instead, it employs a three-stage adaptive process: First, Input-level Calibration uses Feature-Level Linear Modulation (FiLM) to adjust the raw audio and visual features into a neutral space unrelated to the speaker. Then, Interaction-level Gating re-adjusts the trust level for each modality (e.g., voice or facial features) based on the speaker's identity information. Finally, Output-level Regularization maintains the consistency of speaker features in the latent space. Tests on the MELD and IEMOCAP datasets show that our model (ML-SAN) achieves better results, performs exceptionally well in handling challenging tail sentiment categories, and better addresses the diversity of speakers in real-world scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ML-SAN, a multi-level speaker adaptive network that addresses individual differences in emotional expression by using a three-stage adaptive process (input calibration, interaction gating, output regularization) to improve multimodal emotion recognition, achieving state-of-the-art results on MELD and IEMOCAP datasets.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal emotion recognition models treat all individuals with a single "static" model, failing to account for significant variations in how different people express the same emotion (e.g., one person shows happiness facially while another hides it). This "simplification" degrades recognition performance, especially in multi-turn dialogues.
AI.method: ML-SAN employs a three-stage adaptive process: (1) Input-level Calibration uses Feature-Level Linear Modulation (FiLM) to transform raw audio/visual features into a speaker-agnostic neutral space; (2) Interaction-level Gating adjusts modality trust levels (e.g., voice vs. facial features) based on speaker identity; (3) Output-level Regularization enforces consistency of speaker features in the latent space.
AI.result: ML-SAN achieves superior results on MELD and IEMOCAP datasets, with particularly strong performance on challenging tail sentiment categories, and effectively handles speaker diversity in real-world scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ML-SAN effectively addresses the problem of speaker identity information confusion in multimodal emotion recognition by adaptively calibrating features, gating modality contributions, and regularizing outputs based on speaker identity, leading to improved recognition of diverse emotional expression styles.

title: Walking Through Uncertainty: An Empirical Study of Uncertainty Estimation for Audio-Aware Large Language Models
summary: Recent audio-aware large language models (ALLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across diverse audio understanding and reasoning tasks, but they still frequently produce hallucinated or overly confident outputs. While uncertainty estimation has been extensively studied in text-only LLMs, it remains largely unexplored for ALLMs, where audio-conditioned generation introduces additional challenges such as perceptual ambiguity and cross-modal grounding. In this work, we present the first systematic empirical study of uncertainty estimation in ALLMs. We benchmark five representative methods, including predictive entropy, length-normalized entropy, semantic entropy, discrete semantic entropy, and P(True), across multiple models and diverse evaluation settings spanning general audio understanding, reasoning, hallucination detection, and unanswerable question answering. Our results reveal two key findings. First, semantic-level and verification-based methods consistently outperform token-level baselines on general audio reasoning benchmarks. Second, on trustworthiness-oriented benchmarks, the relative effectiveness of uncertainty methods becomes notably more model- and benchmark-dependent, indicating that conclusions drawn from general reasoning settings do not straightforwardly transfer to hallucination and unanswerable-question scenarios. We further explore uncertainty-based adaptive inference as a potential downstream application. We hope this study provides a foundation for future research on reliable, uncertainty-aware audio-language systems.

AI.tldr: First systematic empirical study of uncertainty estimation in audio-aware large language models (ALLMs), benchmarking five methods across general audio reasoning and trustworthiness-oriented tasks, revealing that semantic-level methods outperform token-level ones in general settings but effectiveness is model- and benchmark-dependent in hallucination/unanswerable scenarios.
AI.motivation: While uncertainty estimation is well-studied in text-only LLMs, it remains unexplored for ALLMs, where audio-conditioned generation introduces additional challenges like perceptual ambiguity and cross-modal grounding. The paper aims to fill this gap.
AI.method: Benchmark five uncertainty estimation methods (predictive entropy, length-normalized entropy, semantic entropy, discrete semantic entropy, P(True)) across multiple ALLMs and diverse evaluation settings including general audio understanding, reasoning, hallucination detection, and unanswerable question answering.
AI.result: (1) Semantic-level and verification-based methods outperform token-level baselines on general audio reasoning benchmarks. (2) On trustworthiness-oriented benchmarks, the relative effectiveness of uncertainty methods is notably more model- and benchmark-dependent, showing limited transferability from general settings.
AI.conclusion: This study provides a foundation for future research on reliable, uncertainty-aware audio-language systems, and explores uncertainty-based adaptive inference as a downstream application.

title: Praxy Voice: Voice-Prompt Recovery + BUPS for Commercial-Class Indic TTS from a Frozen Non-Indic Base at Zero Commercial-Training-Data Cost
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Companion paper to PSP benchmark. Code: https://github.com/praxelhq/praxy ; Model: https://huggingface.co/Praxel/praxy-voice-r6 ; Demo: https://huggingface.co/spaces/Praxel/praxy-voice-demo
summary: Commercial TTS systems produce near-native Indic audio, but the best open-source bases (Chatterbox, Indic Parler-TTS, IndicF5) trail them on measured phonological dimensions, and the most widely adopted multilingual base (Chatterbox, 23 languages) does not even tokenise Telugu or Tamil. We ask: what is the minimum intervention that brings such a non-Indic-native base to commercial-class output on Telugu, Tamil, and Hindi, without training a new acoustic decoder and without any commercial TTS training data? We combine three pieces: (1) BUPS, a Brahmic Unified Phoneme Space that deterministically romanises seven Indic scripts to ISO-15919 so Chatterbox's Latin tokeniser can process them; (2) a LoRA adapter on only the text-token predictor (Chatterbox's t3), trained on ~1,220h of licensed Indic audio with a Hindi-proxy language_id; (3) a voice-prompt recovery recipe -- an 8-11s same-language reference clip plus three sampling overrides (exaggeration 0.7, temperature 0.6, min_p 0.1; "Config B") -- that recovers commercial-class acoustic output with no acoustic-decoder training. On Hindi, the LoRA regresses accuracy and we instead use vanilla Chatterbox + Config B, giving a two-branch deployment. Evaluated on 10-utterance pilot sets with the companion PSP benchmark, Praxy Voice matches or slightly leads commercial baselines: 26.7% retroflex collapse on Telugu (vs Sarvam Bulbul 33.3%), 71% Tamil-zha collapse (vs commercial trio's 86%), 0.025 LLM-WER on Hindi (tied with Cartesia Sonic-3). For intra-sentential code-mix we add a third branch (IndicF5 + native-script transliteration) that drops code-mix LLM-WER from 0.80-0.85 to 0.14-0.27 across Hi/Te/Ta. We release R6 LoRA weights (Apache-2.0), inference code and router (MIT), and a Gradio demo.

AI.tldr: Praxy Voice achieves commercial-class Indic TTS (Telugu, Tamil, Hindi) by minimally modifying Chatterbox (a non-Indic-native multilingual base) using: (1) BUPS romanisation for Brahmic scripts, (2) a LoRA adapter on the text-token predictor trained on ~1,220h licensed Indic audio, and (3) a voice-prompt recovery recipe (Config B). It matches/commercial baselines on phonological benchmarks and reduces code-mix LLM-WER via a third branch using IndicF5.
AI.motivation: Commercial TTS systems produce near-native Indic audio, but open-source multilingual bases (e.g., Chatterbox) lag behind on phonological dimensions and fail to even tokenise certain Indic scripts (Telugu, Tamil). The goal is to bridge this gap with minimal intervention — no new acoustic decoder, no commercial TTS training data.
AI.method: Three components: (1) BUPS — deterministic romanisation of seven Brahmic scripts to ISO-15919 for Chatterbox's Latin tokeniser; (2) LoRA adapter on Chatterbox's t3 (text-token predictor) trained on ~1,220h licensed Indic audio with Hindi-proxy language_id; (3) Voice-prompt recovery using an 8–11s same-language reference clip + Config B (exaggeration 0.7, temperature 0.6, min_p 0.1). For Hindi, LoRA degrades accuracy, so vanilla Chatterbox + Config B is used, yielding a two-branch deployment. For code-mix, a third branch uses IndicF5 + native-script transliteration.
AI.result: On Telugu: 26.7% retroflex collapse (vs Sarvam Bulbul 33.3%). On Tamil: 71% zha collapse (vs commercial trio's 86%). On Hindi: 0.025 LLM-WER (tied with Cartesia Sonic-3). Code-mix LLM-WER drops from 0.80–0.85 to 0.14–0.27 across Hindi/Telugu/Tamil.
AI.conclusion: A minimal, non-invasive adaptation of a non-Indic-native multilingual TTS base can match or slightly exceed commercial Indic TTS quality on phonological benchmarks without training a new acoustic decoder or using commercial training data. The approach is extensible to code-mixed speech via a dedicated branch.

title: UNet-Based Fusion and Exponential Moving Average Adaptation for Noise-Robust Speaker Recognition
summary: The joint training of speech enhancement and speaker embedding networks for speaker recognition is widely adopted under noisy acoustic environments. While effective, this paradigm often fails to leverage the generalization and robustness benefits inherent in large-scale speech enhancement pre-training. Moreover, maintaining the speaker information in the denoised speech is not an explicit objective of the speech enhancement process. To address these limitations, we proposed a scalable \textbf{U}Net-based \textbf{F}usion framework (UF-EMA) that considers the noisy and enhanced speech as a multi-channel input, thereby enabling the speaker encoder to exploit speaker information effectively. In addition, an \textbf{E}xponential \textbf{M}oving \textbf{A}verage strategy is applied to a speaker encoder pre-trained on clean speech to mitigate overfitting and facilitate a smooth transition from clean to noisy conditions. Experimental results on multiple noise-contaminated test sets showcase the superiority of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a UNet-based Fusion framework with Exponential Moving Average (UF-EMA) that treats noisy and enhanced speech as multi-channel input for robust speaker recognition, addressing limitations of joint training paradigms by better leveraging pre-trained speech enhancement models and preserving speaker information.
AI.motivation: Existing joint training of speech enhancement and speaker embedding networks fails to exploit the generalization benefits of large-scale speech enhancement pre-training, and speaker information preservation is not an explicit objective in the enhancement process.
AI.method: Proposes a scalable UNet-based Fusion framework (UF-EMA) that treats noisy and enhanced speech as multi-channel input to a speaker encoder, and applies Exponential Moving Average (EMA) to a pre-trained speaker encoder on clean speech to mitigate overfitting and enable smooth transition from clean to noisy conditions.
AI.result: The proposed approach shows superiority over existing methods on multiple noise-contaminated test sets.
AI.conclusion: The UF-EMA framework effectively addresses the limitations of joint training paradigms by fusing noisy and enhanced speech representations and leveraging EMA-based speaker encoder pre-training, achieving robust speaker recognition in noisy environments.

title: PSP: An Interpretable Per-Dimension Accent Benchmark for Indic Text-to-Speech
comment: 8 pages, 7 tables. Companion paper to Praxy Voice (arXiv:submission id - 7506231). Code: https://github.com/praxelhq/psp-eval; Centroids: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Praxel/psp-native-centroids
summary: Standard text-to-speech (TTS) evaluation measures intelligibility (WER, CER) and overall naturalness (MOS, UTMOS) but does not quantify accent. A synthesiser may score well on all four yet sound non-native on features that are phonemic in the target language. For Indic languages, these features include retroflex articulation, aspiration, vowel length, and the Tamil retroflex approximant (letter zha). We present PSP, the Phoneme Substitution Profile, an interpretable, per-phonological-dimension accent benchmark for Indic TTS. PSP decomposes accent into six complementary dimensions: retroflex collapse rate (RR), aspiration fidelity (AF), vowel-length fidelity (LF), Tamil-zha fidelity (ZF), Frechet Audio Distance (FAD), and prosodic signature divergence (PSD). The first four are measured via forced alignment plus native-speaker-centroid acoustic probes over Wav2Vec2-XLS-R layer-9 embeddings; the latter two are corpus-level distributional distances. In this v1 we benchmark four commercial and open-source systems (ElevenLabs v3, Cartesia Sonic-3, Sarvam Bulbul, Indic Parler-TTS) on Hindi, Telugu, and Tamil pilot sets, with a fifth system (Praxy Voice) included on all three languages, plus an R5->R6 case study on Telugu. Three findings: (i) retroflex collapse grows monotonically with phonological difficulty Hindi < Telugu < Tamil (~1%, ~40%, ~68%); (ii) PSP ordering diverges from WER ordering -- commercial WER-leaders do not uniformly lead on retroflex or prosodic fidelity; (iii) no single system is Pareto-optimal across all six dimensions. We release native reference centroids (500 clips per language), 1000-clip embeddings for FAD, 500-clip prosodic feature matrices for PSD, 300-utterance golden sets per language, scoring code under MIT, and centroids under CC-BY. Formal MOS-correlation is deferred to v2; v1 reports five internal-consistency signals plus a native-audio sanity check.

AI.tldr: PSP introduces a phoneme-level accent benchmark for Indic TTS, decomposing accent into six dimensions (retroflex, aspiration, vowel length, Tamil-zha, FAD, prosodic similarity). Evaluations on multiple TTS systems across Hindi, Telugu, and Tamil show retroflex collapse increases with language difficulty, PSP ordering diverges from WER, and no single system is Pareto-optimal.
AI.motivation: Standard TTS evaluation metrics (WER, CER, MOS, UTMOS) measure intelligibility and naturalness but fail to quantify accent, which is critical for Indic languages where non-native phonemic features like retroflex articulation, aspiration, vowel length, and the Tamil retroflex approximant are perceptually important.
AI.method: PSP decomposes accent into six dimensions: retroflex collapse rate (RR), aspiration fidelity (AF), vowel-length fidelity (LF), Tamil-zha fidelity (ZF) — all measured via forced alignment and native-speaker-centroid acoustic probes on Wav2Vec2-XLS-R layer-9 embeddings — plus Frechet Audio Distance (FAD) and prosodic signature divergence (PSD), which are corpus-level distributional distances.
AI.result: (i) Retroflex collapse increases monotonically with phonological difficulty: Hindi ~1%, Telugu ~40%, Tamil ~68%. (ii) PSP ranking diverges from WER ranking — commercial WER leaders do not uniformly lead on retroflex or prosodic fidelity. (iii) No single system is Pareto-optimal across all six dimensions.
AI.conclusion: PSP provides an interpretable, per-dimension accent benchmark that reveals accent weaknesses invisible to standard metrics. Formal MOS correlation is deferred to v2; v1 reports five internal-consistency signals and a native-audio sanity check. Resources are released under open licenses.

title: Stochastic and Dynamic Fundamental Diagram for Mixed Traffic
summary: This study develops a dynamic fundamental diagram (FD) framework tailored to mixed traffic environments comprising automated vehicles (AVs) and human-driven vehicles (HDVs). Describing function analysis is employed to derive approximate linear transfer functions for nonlinear HDV car-following models. A sequence-based stochastic dynamic FD is then formulated for mixed platoons, enabling the evaluation of hysteresis in the evolution of flow-density relations across different vehicle sequencing scenarios and AV penetration levels. Monte Carlo simulation results reveal that (i) differences in AV-HDV sequencing significantly alter the size of traffic hysteresis loops; and (ii) higher AV shares generally dampen hysteresis magnitude and variability, yet the net impact depends on how AVs are distributed within the platoon. The results suggest that traffic hysteresis in mixed environments is governed not only by the composition of AVs and HDVs, but also by how their interactions unfold through sequencing.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a dynamic fundamental diagram framework for mixed traffic (AVs + HDVs), using describing function analysis and stochastic modeling to show that both AV penetration levels and AV-HDV sequencing significantly affect traffic hysteresis in flow-density relations.
AI.motivation: Existing fundamental diagrams assume homogeneous traffic and fail to capture hysteresis in mixed environments; this study aims to understand how AV-HDV interactions and sequencing affect traffic flow dynamics.
AI.method: Describing function analysis to linearize nonlinear HDV car-following models; sequence-based stochastic dynamic FD formulation; Monte Carlo simulations across various sequencing scenarios and AV penetration levels.
AI.result: (i) AV-HDV sequencing significantly alters hysteresis loop size; (ii) higher AV shares generally reduce hysteresis magnitude and variability, but the net effect depends on AV distribution within the platoon.
AI.conclusion: Traffic hysteresis in mixed environments is governed by both AV/HDV composition and their sequencing/interaction patterns, not just penetration rates alone.

title: Step-Audio-R1.5 Technical Report
summary: Recent advancements in large audio language models have extended Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into the auditory domain, enabling models to tackle increasingly complex acoustic and spoken tasks. To elicit and sustain these extended reasoning chains, the prevailing paradigm -- driven by the success of text-based reasoning models -- overwhelmingly relies on Reinforcement Learning with Verified Rewards (RLVR). However, as models are strictly optimized to distill rich, continuous auditory contexts into isolated, verifiable text labels, a fundamental question arises: are we fostering true audio intelligence, or merely reducing a continuous sensory medium into a discrete puzzle? We identify this as the "verifiable reward trap." While RLVR yields remarkable scores on standardized objective benchmarks, it systematically degrades the real-world conversational feel of audio models. By prioritizing isolated correctness over acoustic nuance, RLVR reduces dynamic interactions to mechanical "answering machines," severely compromising prosodic naturalness, emotional continuity, and user immersion, particularly in long-turn dialogues. To bridge the gap between mechanical objective verification and genuine sensory empathy, we introduce Step-Audio-R1.5, marking a paradigm shift toward Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) in audio reasoning. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that Step-Audio-R1.5 not only maintains robust analytical reasoning but profoundly transforms the interactive experience, redefining the boundaries of deeply immersive long-turn spoken dialogue.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a "verifiable reward trap" in audio language models, where Reinforcement Learning with Verified Rewards (RLVR) achieves high benchmark scores but degrades natural conversational quality. To counter this, the authors propose Step-Audio-R1.5, shifting to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to preserve both reasoning capability and immersive, natural spoken interaction.
AI.motivation: While RLVR-driven CoT reasoning excels on objective audio benchmarks, it systematically harms real-world conversational naturalness (prosody, emotional continuity, immersion), reducing models to "answering machines." The paper questions whether current methods foster true audio intelligence or merely overfit to discrete label verification.
AI.method: The authors propose Step-Audio-R1.5, which shifts the training paradigm from RLVR to RLHF, incorporating human feedback to optimize for both analytical reasoning and acoustic naturalness in long-turn spoken dialogue.
AI.result: Step-Audio-R1.5 maintains robust analytical reasoning while significantly improving conversational quality, including prosodic naturalness, emotional continuity, and user immersion in extended dialogues.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that RLHF offers a viable path to bridge objective verification and sensory empathy, redefining immersive long-turn spoken interaction without sacrificing reasoning performance.

title: SymphonyGen: 3D Hierarchical Orchestral Generation with Controllable Harmony Skeleton
summary: Generating symphonic music requires simultaneously managing high-level structural form and dense, multi-track orchestration. Existing symbolic models often struggle with a "complexity-control imbalance", in which scaling bottlenecks limit long-term granular steerability. We present SymphonyGen, a 3D hierarchical framework for contemporary cinematic orchestration. SymphonyGen employs a cascading decoder architecture that decomposes the Bar, Track, and Event axes, improving computational efficiency and scalability over conventional 1D or 2D models. We introduce "short-score" conditioning via a beat-quantized multi-voice harmony skeleton, enabling outline control while preserving textural diversity. The model is further refined using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a cross-modal audio-perceptual reward, aligning symbolic output with modern acoustic expectations. Additionally, we implement a dissonance-averse sampling algorithm to suppress unintended tonal clashes during inference. Objective evaluations show that both reinforcement learning and dissonance-averse sampling effectively enhance harmonic cleanliness while maintaining melodic expression. Subjective evaluations demonstrate that SymphonyGen outperforms baselines in musicality and preference for orchestral music generation. Demo page: https://symphonygen.github.io/

AI.tldr: SymphonyGen is a 3D hierarchical framework (Bar, Track, Event axes) for cinematic orchestral music generation that uses cascading decoders, short-score conditioning, GRPO with audio-perceptual reward, and dissonance-averse sampling to achieve better complexity control, harmonic cleanliness, and musicality than existing symbolic models.
AI.motivation: Existing symbolic music generation models suffer from a "complexity-control imbalance" where scaling bottlenecks limit long-term granular steerability when generating symphonic music that requires simultaneously managing high-level structural form and dense multi-track orchestration.
AI.method: SymphonyGen uses: 1) a 3D hierarchical cascading decoder architecture decomposing Bar, Track, and Event axes for better scalability; 2) "short-score" conditioning via beat-quantized multi-voice harmony skeleton for outline control; 3) Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with cross-modal audio-perceptual reward; 4) dissonance-averse sampling algorithm to suppress tonal clashes.
AI.result: Objective evaluations show both reinforcement learning and dissonance-averse sampling effectively enhance harmonic cleanliness while maintaining melodic expression. Subjective evaluations demonstrate SymphonyGen outperforms baselines in musicality and preference for orchestral music generation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed 3D hierarchical framework with short-score conditioning, GRPO fine-tuning, and dissonance-averse sampling successfully addresses the complexity-control imbalance in symbolic orchestral generation, achieving superior musicality and preference over existing approaches.

title: A Quantitative Framework for Navigating Controller Design Tradeoffs under Computational Constraints
summary: Computational constraints permeate the controller design process, and yet are rarely treated as explicit design constraints. Towards addressing this gap, we propose a quantitative framework that captures the effects of common design approximations, such as model order reduction, temporal discretization, horizon truncation, and solver accuracy, on both controller performance and computational requirements. Our framework highlights that these approximations are tunable parameters within an overall controller design process. By leveraging incremental input-to-state stability, we show that bounding the aggregate effects of these approximations reduces to verifying a design-dependent sector bound on the difference between the deployed policy and an idealized baseline, with stability enforced via a small-gain condition. We operationalize these insights via a Design Meta-Problem in which the performance gap is minimized subject to stability, real-time compute, and timing constraints. Finally, we instantiate the framework on a receding horizon LQR case study, and demonstrate a principled near-optimal navigation of tradeoffs among sampling rate, model order, horizon length, and solver iterations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantitative framework for treating computational constraints as explicit design parameters in controller design. It captures the effects of common approximations (model reduction, temporal discretization, horizon truncation, solver accuracy) on performance and computational requirements, using incremental input-to-state stability and small-gain conditions to bound their aggregate effects. A Design Meta-Problem minimizes performance gap under stability, real-time, and timing constraints, demonstrated on a receding horizon LQR case study.
AI.motivation: Computational constraints permeate controller design but are rarely treated as explicit design constraints. The paper aims to address this gap by providing a framework that quantifies and incorporates these constraints directly into the design process.
AI.method: The paper uses incremental input-to-state stability to bound aggregate effects of approximations via a sector bound on the difference between deployed policy and idealized baseline, enforced by a small-gain condition. It formulates a Design Meta-Problem minimizing performance gap under stability, real-time compute, and timing constraints.
AI.result: The framework is instantiated on a receding horizon LQR case study, demonstrating principled near-optimal navigation of tradeoffs among sampling rate, model order, horizon length, and solver iterations.
AI.conclusion: Computational approximations in controller design can be treated as tunable parameters, enabling systematic tradeoff navigation between performance and computational requirements through a unified quantitative framework.

title: Interval Observer Design Using Observability Decomposition for Detectable Linear Systems
comment: 23rd IFAC World Congress, Busan, South Korea, Aug. 2026
summary: We provide a systematic interval observer design method for detectable linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, where a part of the state is observable from the measured output. An observability-based invertible LTI transformation decomposes the state into two parts. The first part is decoupled from the other and observable from the output, while the second is affected by the first, does not appear in the output, but is detectable. A Sylvester-based LTI interval observer is designed for the first part. For the second part, a Jordan-based linear time-varying interval observer is built, treating the interaction from the first part as inputs with known bounds. The intervals in the original coordinates are constructed either by inverting the decomposition online for the intervals in the transformed coordinates or by directly implementing the observer written in the original coordinates. Academic examples illustrate the interest of our approach.

AI.tldr: A systematic interval observer design method for detectable LTI systems using a state decomposition approach, combining a Sylvester-based LTI observer for the observable part and a Jordan-based time-varying observer for the detectable part.
AI.motivation: To provide a systematic interval observer design for detectable LTI systems where only part of the state is observable from the output, addressing the gap in existing methods that often assume stronger observability conditions.
AI.method: Uses an observability-based invertible LTI transformation to decompose the state into an observable part (decoupled from the other) and a detectable part (affected by the first, not in output). A Sylvester-based LTI interval observer is designed for the observable part, and a Jordan-based linear time-varying interval observer is built for the detectable part, treating interactions as bounded inputs.
AI.result: Intervals in original coordinates are constructed either by inverting the decomposition online for transformed coordinate intervals or by directly implementing the observer in original coordinates. Academic examples validate the approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method offers a systematic and effective interval observer design for detectable LTI systems, demonstrated through academic examples.

title: A Class AAA Solar Testbed for Reproducible Long-Term Characterization of Energy-Harvesting Systems
summary: Energy harvesting promises maintenance-free operation of wireless sensor nodes but introduces strong dependencies on stochastic and deployment-specific environmental conditions. In particular, solar-powered systems are highly sensitive to variations in irradiance and spectral composition, which complicates system-level design, parameter tuning, and reliable verification. This work presents a solar testbed in which active control via Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) enables stable and repeatable illumination conditions for evaluating ultra-low-power energy harvesting systems. The proposed LED-based solar testbed provides spectrally configurable illumination over a wide dynamic range, from 5.7 mW/m2 to 908 kW/m2. It achieves Class AAA performance according to IEC 60904-9, with a spectral match below 1.3% and a spatial non-uniformity below 1.28% over a 16.5 cm x 16.5 cm test area. The long-term irradiance instability remains below 0.6%. Closed-loop control using integrated illuminance and spectral sensors ensures high temporal stability, while a temperature-controlled DUT stage supports long-term experiments. Experimental results demonstrate high repeatability and suitability for systematic laboratory characterization of solar energy harvesting systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an LED-based solar testbed with Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) control that provides stable, repeatable, and spectrally configurable illumination (5.7 mW/m² to 908 kW/m²) for evaluating ultra-low-power solar energy harvesting systems. It achieves Class AAA per IEC 60904-9 with <1.3% spectral match, <1.28% spatial non-uniformity over 16.5 cm × 16.5 cm, and <0.6% long-term irradiance instability.
AI.motivation: Energy harvesting promises maintenance-free wireless sensor nodes but introduces strong dependencies on stochastic and deployment-specific environmental conditions. Solar-powered systems are highly sensitive to variations in irradiance and spectral composition, complicating system-level design, parameter tuning, and reliable verification. A stable, repeatable testbed is needed to address these challenges.
AI.method: The authors developed an LED-based solar testbed with active Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) control. It uses closed-loop control with integrated illuminance and spectral sensors for high temporal stability, and a temperature-controlled DUT stage. The system provides spectrally configurable illumination over a wide dynamic range.
AI.result: The testbed achieves Class AAA performance per IEC 60904-9: spectral match <1.3%, spatial non-uniformity <1.28% over 16.5 cm × 16.5 cm, long-term irradiance instability <0.6%. Illumination range spans from 5.7 mW/m² to 908 kW/m².
AI.conclusion: Experimental results demonstrate high repeatability and suitability for systematic laboratory characterization of solar energy harvesting systems. The HIL-controlled testbed enables stable and repeatable illumination conditions essential for reliable evaluation of ultra-low-power energy harvesting systems.

title: A Novel Two-Step Approach for Reactive Power Demand Calculation Using Integrated Voltage Stability Analysis
summary: The assessment of reactive power demand plays an instrumental role in power system planning. This paper presents a methodology for calculating reactive power demand based on a two-step approach. Unlike existing methodologies in the literature that focus primarily on optimization of reactive power compensation equipment placement and sizing through single-simulation approaches, this methodology directly calculates the actual reactive power demand through a comprehensive back-to-back simulation framework. While existing methods address either long-term or short-term voltage stability using either steady-state analysis or individual dynamic simulations, the proposed approach integrates both stability assessments sequentially through iterative Quasi-Dynamic Simulation, Q-V analysis and dynamic simulation. Furthermore, this methodology employs comprehensive time-series analysis over a full annual period (8760 hours) with multi-criteria violation assessment (number, severity and duration of voltage violations). In the final section of this paper, a case study was conducted to demonstrate the application of the proposed methodology. Simulations were performed to validate the effectiveness of the methodology, with the results showing that all buses with voltage issues were successfully addressed and finally the total reactive power demand across the network was calculated.

AI.tldr: A two-step methodology for calculating reactive power demand using back-to-back simulations (Quasi-Dynamic Simulation, Q-V analysis, and dynamic simulation) with annual time-series analysis and multi-criteria violation assessment, validated on a case study.
AI.motivation: Reactive power demand assessment is critical for power system planning, but existing methods focus on optimizing compensation equipment placement via single simulations and address either long-term or short-term voltage stability in isolation.
AI.method: A two-step approach using a comprehensive back-to-back simulation framework integrating Quasi-Dynamic Simulation, Q-V analysis, and dynamic simulation sequentially; includes full annual period (8760 hours) time-series analysis with multi-criteria violation assessment (number, severity, duration).
AI.result: All buses with voltage issues were successfully addressed, and the total reactive power demand across the network was calculated.
AI.conclusion: The proposed methodology effectively calculates actual reactive power demand by integrating both long-term and short-term voltage stability assessments, outperforming single-simulation approaches in the literature.

title: On Distributed Control of Continuum Swarms: Local Controllers as Differential Operators
summary: We study the problem of distributed control of large-scale robotic swarms which can be modeled as continuum densities evolving under the continuity equation. We propose a formalization of distributed controllers as (generally nonlinear) differential operators, in which control inputs depend only on local information about the state and environment. This perspective yields a fully local, PDE-based framework for analysis and design. We apply this framework to the problem of stabilizing a swarm density around an arbitrary target density, and investigate fundamental limitations of low-order distributed controllers in achieving this goal. In particular, we show that controllers which act in a purely pointwise manner are incompatible with natural system symmetries and strong forms of stability, and must rely on mixing-type behavior to achieve stabilization. In contrast, we present a simple first-order control law which achieves stabilization and enjoys substantially stronger properties.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a PDE-based framework for distributed control of robotic swarms modeled as continuum densities, analyzes fundamental limitations of pointwise controllers, and presents a first-order control law that achieves stabilization with stronger properties.
AI.motivation: To develop a formal, local, PDE-based framework for analyzing and designing distributed controllers for large-scale robotic swarms, and to understand fundamental limitations of low-order distributed controllers in stabilizing swarm densities.
AI.method: The authors formalize distributed controllers as nonlinear differential operators that depend only on local information, applying this PDE-based framework to the problem of stabilizing a swarm density around an arbitrary target density.
AI.result: Pointwise controllers are incompatible with natural system symmetries and strong stability, requiring mixing-type behavior. A first-order control law achieves stabilization with substantially stronger properties.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables systematic analysis of distributed swarm control, revealing fundamental limitations of low-order controllers while demonstrating that a simple first-order law can overcome these limitations.

title: Behaviour-aware Hybrid Architecture for Trust-driven Transmissions
summary: Reliable and secure communication is essential for mission-critical aerospace and defence operations involving autonomous platforms such as Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), satellites, and ground control systems. In contested or dynamic environments, communication links are frequently exposed to jamming, interference, and cyberattacks, making network resilience a key operational requirement. This paper presents a trust-aware Software-Defined Networking (SDN) framework that enables secure, low-latency failover between heterogeneous communication channels. The proposed architecture integrates a high-bandwidth primary link (e.g., satellite or tactical LTE) with a low-power fallback channel (e.g., RF or mesh), managed by an SDN controller that enforces zero-trust routing policies. A real-time Intrusion Detection System (IDS) continuously updates node trust scores; when trust or link reliability degrades, the controller autonomously switches traffic to the secondary channel, ensuring uninterrupted connectivity. Simulation results in a Mininet-based test environment demonstrate sub-5 ms failover latency, efficient flow installation, and significant reduction in packet loss compared with conventional single-channel or static routing systems. The proposed framework provides a scalable and resilient communication backbone for next-generation aerospace networks, enhancing mission reliability, cyber defence, and autonomous coordination across distributed aerial and space assets.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a trust-aware SDN framework for aerospace/defence networks that enables autonomous failover between primary (e.g., satellite, LTE) and secondary (e.g., RF, mesh) communication channels based on real-time trust scores and IDS alerts. Simulations demonstrate sub-5 ms failover latency and reduced packet loss.
AI.motivation: Reliable and secure communication is critical for autonomous aerospace platforms (UAVs, satellites, ground systems) operating in contested environments where jamming, interference, and cyberattacks threaten network resilience.
AI.method: A trust-aware SDN architecture with zero-trust routing policies, dual heterogeneous channels (high-bandwidth primary + low-power fallback), a real-time IDS updating node trust scores, and an SDN controller that autonomously switches traffic upon trust/link degradation.
AI.result: Mininet-based simulations show sub-5 ms failover latency, efficient flow installation, and significant packet loss reduction compared to conventional single-channel or static routing systems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a scalable, resilient communication backbone for next-generation aerospace networks, enhancing mission reliability, cyber defence, and autonomous coordination across distributed aerial and space assets.

title: Distributed adaptive estimation for stochastic large regression models
summary: This paper studies the distributed adaptiveestimation problems for stochastic large regression modelswith an infinite number of parameters. By constructing a re-cursive local cost function, we propose a novel distributedrecursive least squares algorithm to estimate the unknownsystem parameters, where the growth rate of regressors'dimension is characterized by a non-decreasing positivefunction. The almost sure convergence of the proposedalgorithm is established under a cooperative excitationcondition, which incorporates the temporal information andthe spatial information to reflect the cooperative effectamong multiple agents. Moreover, we analyze the predic-tion error by establishing the asymptotic upper boundof the accumulated regret without any excitation condi-tions. The main difficulty of theoretical analysis lies in howto analyze properties of the product of non-independentand non-stationary random matrices, whose dimensionschange over time simultaneously. Some techniques, suchas stochastic Lyapunov function, double-array martingaletheory and algebraic graph theory, are employed to dealwith the above issue. Our theoretical results are derivedwithout imposing independence or stationarity assump-tions on the regression vectors, thereby not excluding thecorrelated feedback signals.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a distributed recursive least squares algorithm for stochastic large regression models with infinite parameters, establishes almost sure convergence under cooperative excitation, and analyzes regret bounds without excitation conditions, handling time-varying random matrices using stochastic Lyapunov functions and martingale theory.
AI.motivation: To solve distributed adaptive estimation problems for stochastic large regression models with an infinite number of parameters, where the regressor dimension grows over time and agents cooperate in a distributed network.
AI.method: Constructs a recursive local cost function and proposes a distributed recursive least squares (DRLS) algorithm. Theoretical analysis uses stochastic Lyapunov functions, double-array martingale theory, and algebraic graph theory to handle non-independent, non-stationary random matrices with time-varying dimensions.
AI.result: Establishes almost sure convergence of the DRLS algorithm under a cooperative excitation condition that incorporates temporal and spatial information. Also provides an asymptotic upper bound for accumulated regret without requiring any excitation conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DRLS algorithm converges almost surely under cooperative excitation, and regret bounds hold even without excitation conditions. Results do not require independence or stationarity assumptions on regression vectors, allowing correlated feedback signals.

title: Complex-Vector Power and Cross-Phase Unbalance in Three-Phase Systems
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, submitted to IEEE Trans. on Power Delivery
summary: Unbalanced three-phase systems still lack a compact phasor-domain representation of power that makes phase asymmetry explicit while remaining consistent with established apparent-power definitions. This paper addresses that point through a complex-vector power formulation for sinusoidal steady-state operation. The proposed representation supplements the classical dot-product expression of complex power with the cross product of voltage and current phasors, thereby retaining the usual active and reactive terms while making explicit a cross-phase unbalance vector that captures antisymmetric interphase relations. In this way, apparent power is separated into intraphase and cross-phase contributions, and its norm is preserved under the power-invariant Fortescue transformation. The formulation is extended to three-phase four-wire systems by introducing equivalent coordinates that preserve the effective apparent-power norm for the chosen voltage reference. Only standard complex numbers and matrices are required. Numerical examples show operating conditions in which a non-negligible part of the apparent-power structure is associated with cross-phase unbalance and cannot be inferred from active and reactive power alone. The proposed formulation thus provides a compact phasor-based descriptor of unbalance that complements established apparent-power theories by making explicit a component that is not accessible from scalar apparent-power representations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a complex-vector power formulation for unbalanced three-phase systems that adds a cross-product term to the classical complex power, introducing a cross-phase unbalance vector to capture antisymmetric interphase relations. This separates apparent power into intraphase and cross-phase contributions, preserves norm under Fortescue transformation, and extends to four-wire systems using equivalent coordinates.
AI.motivation: Unbalanced three-phase systems lack a compact phasor-domain power representation that makes phase asymmetry explicit while remaining consistent with established apparent-power definitions.
AI.method: The paper supplements the classical dot-product expression of complex power with the cross product of voltage and current phasors, forming a complex-vector power formulation. This separates apparent power into intraphase and cross-phase contributions, with the cross-phase unbalance vector capturing antisymmetric interphase relations. The formulation preserves norm under power-invariant Fortescue transformation and extends to three-phase four-wire systems using equivalent coordinates.
AI.result: Numerical examples demonstrate operating conditions where a non-negligible portion of apparent-power structure is associated with cross-phase unbalance, which cannot be inferred from active and reactive power alone.
AI.conclusion: The proposed formulation provides a compact phasor-based descriptor of unbalance that complements established apparent-power theories by making explicit a component not accessible from scalar apparent-power representations.

title: Multi-layer barrier adaptation of the discrete-time super-twisting controller
comment: 6 pages, accepted to 18th International Workshop on Variable Structure Systems
summary: In digital sliding mode control implementations, discretization-induced chattering and inter-sample blindness can severely degrade the closed-loop performance, especially in case of fast perturbations. This paper addresses these challenges for a discrete-time implementation of the super-twisting sliding mode controller. Building upon recent results on barrier-function-modulated super-twisting algorithms, a nested architecture employing multiple barriers is discretized using an eigenvalue-based exact matching approach. The resulting discrete-time controller preserves the adaptive and robustness properties established in continuous time, while ensuring consistent stability behavior at the sampling level. The proposed framework is validated through numerical simulations. The results highlight the effectiveness of multi-layer barrier adaptation for discrete-time sliding mode control applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a discrete-time implementation of the super-twisting sliding mode controller using a nested multi-layer barrier-function architecture with eigenvalue-based exact matching discretization to eliminate chattering and inter-sample blindness, preserving continuous-time robustness and stability.
AI.motivation: Discretization-induced chattering and inter-sample blindness in digital sliding mode control severely degrade closed-loop performance, especially under fast perturbations.
AI.method: A nested multi-layer barrier-function-modulated super-twisting algorithm is discretized using an eigenvalue-based exact matching approach.
AI.result: The discrete-time controller preserves continuous-time adaptive and robustness properties while ensuring consistent stability at the sampling level, validated through numerical simulations.
AI.conclusion: Multi-layer barrier adaptation is effective for discrete-time sliding mode control applications, mitigating chattering and inter-sample blindness.

title: Local Shifted Passivity Analysis of the Single-Machine Infinite-Bus System
summary: This letter presents a shifted passivity analysis of the single-machine infinite-bus system in the stationary ($αβ$) reference frame. We study the attractivity of a periodic synchronous steady state with constant rotor frequency and formulate shifted passivity with respect to this motion. A port-Hamiltonian representation of the machine dynamics is used to construct a local shifted passivity condition from the error Hamiltonian and a correction term adapted to the synchronous steady state. For the infinite-bus interconnection, the resulting dissipation inequality leads to a sufficient stability condition expressed in terms of field excitation magnitude, damping, inertia, and steady-state current. This condition implies local asymptotic stability of the synchronous steady state and yields a sublevel-set estimate of its region of attraction under an additional small-inertia condition. A distinctive feature of the analysis is that it preserves the periodic structure of the rotor angle and provides a compact passivity-based stability certificate for the stationary-frame model.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a shifted passivity analysis of a single-machine infinite-bus system in the stationary (αβ) reference frame, deriving a local stability condition for the synchronous steady state using a port-Hamiltonian representation and dissipation inequality, with a sublevel-set estimate of the region of attraction under a small-inertia condition.
AI.motivation: To establish a passivity-based stability certificate for the single-machine infinite-bus system that preserves the periodic structure of the rotor angle and works in the stationary reference frame.
AI.method: A port-Hamiltonian representation of machine dynamics is used to construct a local shifted passivity condition from the error Hamiltonian and a correction term adapted to the synchronous steady state. A dissipation inequality yields a sufficient stability condition expressed in terms of field excitation magnitude, damping, inertia, and steady-state current.
AI.result: The derived condition implies local asymptotic stability of the synchronous steady state and yields a sublevel-set estimate of its region of attraction under an additional small-inertia condition.
AI.conclusion: The analysis preserves the periodic structure of the rotor angle and provides a compact passivity-based stability certificate for the stationary-frame model.

title: Backstepping Observer for the Quasilinear Heat Equation with Linear Design Gains: Beyond Local Stability
comment: This is a working document of a work in progress
summary: We consider the one-dimensional quasilinear heat equation with state-dependent heat capacity and thermal conductivity, and design a boundary-output observer based on the backstepping design for a linear heat equation with constant coefficients. Viewing the quasilinear system as a perturbation of the linear one, we establish exponential stability of the origin for the observation error dynamics in $H^1$, with an explicit region of attraction depending on the system parameters, observer gains, and the mismatch between the nonlinear diffusivity and the constant design diffusivity. Importantly, the observation error converges to zero rather than merely to a neighborhood scaling with this mismatch, even though, in contrast to backstepping-based stabilization of nonlinear PDEs, the mismatch need not decay along trajectories and may remain bounded away from zero, acting as a persistent state-dependent multiplicative perturbation. A technical challenge was to perform a sufficiently-fine Lyapunov analysis that does not yield overly conservative results such as mere boundedness of the observation error. Interestingly, while in the linear case the relationship between one of the backstepping observer gains and the convergence rate is monotonic, we show that in the nonlinear setting this is no longer the case: there may exist an optimal value of that gain, beyond which further increases deteriorate the system's performance. Such behavior cannot be predicted without our analysis: one might expect a priori the decay rate to be freely tunable at the expense of a region of attraction that shrinks to zero as the prescribed rate tends to infinity. However, our Lyapunov analysis (supported by numerical experiments) reveals that this intuition is incorrect.

AI.tldr: This paper designs a boundary-output observer for a 1D quasilinear heat equation with state-dependent coefficients, using backstepping for a linear constant-coefficient heat equation as a baseline. Despite the persistent nonlinear mismatch, the observation error converges to zero in $H^1$ with an explicit region of attraction. It also reveals a non-monotonic relationship between an observer gain and convergence rate, contradicting the linear intuition.
AI.motivation: Extend backstepping observer design from linear PDEs to quasilinear heat equations with state-dependent heat capacity and thermal conductivity, where standard linearization approaches would only guarantee boundedness rather than convergence to zero of the observation error.
AI.method: The quasilinear system is treated as a perturbation of a linear constant-coefficient heat equation. A backstepping-based observer is designed for the linear part, and a Lyapunov analysis is performed to establish exponential stability in $H^1$ for the nonlinear observation error dynamics, carefully deriving an explicit region of attraction.
AI.result: Exponential stability of the observation error origin is achieved despite a persistent, state-dependent multiplicative perturbation that does not decay along trajectories. The convergence rate is not monotonic with respect to a backstepping observer gain; an optimal gain exists beyond which performance deteriorates.
AI.conclusion: The analysis provides non-conservative stability guarantees for nonlinear PDE observation, revealing nonlinear phenomena (non-monotonic gain-rate relationship) absent in the linear theory and not predictable by naive intuition.
